questions.key_step: Split into 4-digit numbers starting with 7 or 8 and all 5-digit numbers.
questions.justification: Two direct cases of digit counting with no repetition; one familiar move (fix the leading digit). Options available.

questions.key_step: Thousands digit must be 5, 7 or 9.
questions.justification: One decision (leading digit at least 5) then a plain arrangement count.

questions.key_step: Count the words that start with each smaller prefix, then add 1.
questions.justification: Standard dictionary-rank procedure with distinct letters; routine but several steps.

questions.key_step: Write both permutations with factorials and cancel to a quadratic.
questions.justification: Single formula ${}^nP_r=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!}$ then simplification; no counting idea needed.

questions.key_step: Even digits fill the four even places; odd digits fill the five odd places.
questions.justification: Two independent multiset arrangements multiplied; familiar pattern.

questions.key_step: Split by the number of language courses chosen: 2, 1 or 0.
questions.justification: Case split on at most two language courses; each case a product of two binomials.

questions.key_step: Group 1..25 by remainder mod 5 and pair remainders summing to 0 mod 5.
questions.justification: Needs the residue-class idea and care with the equal-remainder pair; ordered/unordered subtlety.

questions.key_step: List the admissible (red, white, orange) counts adding to 5.
questions.justification: Enumerate three compositions and multiply binomials; precision risk moderate.

questions.key_step: Count numbers above 35337 prefix by prefix, remembering every larger digit option at each place.
questions.justification: Rank counting with repetition; easy to omit a branch (the PDF does).

questions.key_step: Strictly increasing digit strings from 1..9 correspond to 6-subsets; count by prefix.
questions.justification: Recognise subsets, then prefix counting with binomials; two stages.

questions.key_step: Last digit 5 and digit sum a multiple of 3; list the multisets for the first three digits.
questions.justification: Combines two divisibility rules and requires an organised case list; slips are easy.

questions.key_step: Fix the last digit as 1, 3 or 5 and arrange the remaining six.
questions.justification: Three direct cases of multiset arrangement.

questions.key_step: Count numbers smaller than 42923 prefix by prefix (leading digit cannot be 0).
questions.justification: Prefix counting with six digit options at each place and a zero restriction on the first place.

questions.key_step: Glue the vowels into one block, arrange block and consonants, then arrange inside the block.
questions.justification: Block method with two repeated-letter factors; precision on the multiplicities.

questions.key_step: Shift the variables to non-negative and apply stars and bars.
questions.justification: One standard technique (substitution then ${}^{n+r-1}C_{r-1}$).

questions.key_step: Last digit is forced to be 4; the digit-sum condition fixes the last free digit.
questions.justification: One observation (only 4 is even) then a product count with a mod-3 closure.

questions.key_step: Expand both binomials and cancel to a linear equation in $n$.
questions.justification: One formula use and a linear equation.

questions.key_step: For each letter count the unused smaller letters times the factorial of the places left.
questions.justification: Standard rank-of-word procedure with six distinct letters.

questions.key_step: Seat the boys round the table first; the seven gaps then hold the five girls.
questions.justification: Circular permutation plus gap method; standard but needs both ideas.

questions.key_step: Glue the five vowels into a block and arrange block plus seven consonants.
questions.justification: Block method with repeated letters in both groups.

questions.key_step: Total arrangements minus those with C and S glued, then divide by 6!.
questions.justification: Complement with a repeated-letter multiset and a final simplification to k.

questions.key_step: Only the size pattern (3,3,2) is possible; choose which car takes 2 persons.
questions.justification: Identify the single size pattern, then multinomial with a choice of car.

questions.key_step: Total solutions minus those with two equal values minus the all-equal one.
questions.justification: Stars and bars with an exclusion of equal coordinates; careful count of the equal cases.

questions.key_step: Count the smaller unused letters at each place times the factorial of the places left.
questions.justification: Standard rank procedure with five distinct letters.

questions.key_step: Split by last digit $0$ or $5$ and count the allowed leading digits.
questions.justification: Two cases coupled through the shared digit 5; routine but needs care.

questions.key_step: Alphabetical order ADMNOY; count smaller prefixes block by block.
questions.justification: Standard rank procedure, six distinct letters.

questions.key_step: List the digit multisets whose sum is a multiple of 3 and count their arrangements.
questions.justification: Systematic enumeration of sums; omissions are likely but numbers are small.

questions.key_step: Give each child one orange first, then distribute the remaining 17 freely.
questions.justification: Direct stars-and-bars with one shift.

questions.key_step: Choose the two vowels and two consonants from the distinct letters, then arrange all four.
questions.justification: Select then arrange; one familiar move.

questions.key_step: Apply Legendre's formula for the prime 3.
questions.justification: Single formula (Legendre) applied once.

questions.key_step: Count matches for $n$ couples: two men, two non-wives, and two pairings.
questions.justification: Needs a model of a mixed-doubles match and an equation solved by recognising $5\cdot6\cdot7\cdot8$.

questions.key_step: Use inclusion-exclusion; the two strings share no digit, so both can occur together.
questions.justification: Inclusion-exclusion with glued blocks; the intersection term is easy to forget.

questions.key_step: Find each digit's total contribution per place; the same column sum applies to all four places.
questions.justification: Standard place-value sum with a repeated digit; arithmetic precision.

questions.key_step: Apply the derangement formula $D_n=n!\sum(-1)^k/k!$.
questions.justification: One standard formula applied once.

questions.key_step: A.P. triples can only be abc or cba; count 'at least once' by inclusion-exclusion over overlapping occurrences, not by gluing one block.
questions.justification: Overlapping occurrences of two patterns with exact multiplicity; the obvious block method over-counts, and there is no option to check against.

questions.key_step: Shift to $y_i=x_i-1\in\{0,..,3\}$ with sum $5$ and remove the solutions with some $y_i\ge4$.
questions.justification: Bounded stars and bars through a generating function; one correction term.

questions.key_step: Unit digit $2$ or $4$; then count pairs of first two digits by their residue sum mod $3$.
questions.justification: Two divisibility rules with residue bookkeeping; small numbers.

questions.key_step: Fix the common pair sum $s$; the digit $7$ must lie in one of the two pairs.
questions.justification: Casework on the common sum with distinctness and the 'greatest digit is 7' condition; precision matters and no options.

questions.key_step: Recognise $\frac{24!}{(4!)^6\,6!}$ and $\frac{120!}{(5!)^{24}\,24!}$ as counts of divisions into groups.
questions.justification: The quotient has to be recognised as a grouping count; unfamiliar way to test integrality.

questions.key_step: Identical books into identical shelves means partitions of $8$ into at most $4$ parts.
questions.justification: Recognise partitions of an integer and list them without a miss.

questions.key_step: Give each child $2$ apples first, then distribute the remaining $15$ freely.
questions.justification: One shift then stars and bars.

questions.key_step: Use Pascal's rule twice to collapse the sum to ${}^8C_{m+2}$ and compare with ${}^8C_3$.
questions.justification: Pascal's identity twice plus a ratio of permutations; routine algebra and evaluation.

questions.key_step: Count partitions of $5$ people into at most $4$ groups by their size pattern.
questions.justification: Needs the size-pattern enumeration with identical offices; several patterns each with its own multinomial.

questions.key_step: Alphabetical order $E,G,N,T,T,W,Y$; count blocks of smaller prefixes with the repeated $T$ in mind.
questions.justification: Dictionary rank with a repeated letter; block sizes need the $2!$ corrections.

questions.key_step: After taking 4 from each section, the remaining 3 questions follow patterns $(1,1,1)$, $(3,0,0)$, $(2,1,0)$ (respecting section sizes).
questions.justification: Five-pattern casework with a different binomial product each time; precision risk and no options.

questions.key_step: Classify the 4-letter selections by repetition type: all different, one pair, two pairs, a triple.
questions.justification: Four selection types with repeated letters ($I$ thrice, $T$ twice); precision risk.

questions.key_step: Fix $z$; the pairs $(x,y)$ number $\lfloor\frac{42-3z}{2}\rfloor+1$, then sum over $z$.
questions.justification: Sum of an arithmetic-like series from fixing one variable; arithmetic precision needed.

questions.key_step: Parallel pairs give no point and concurrent pairs give only one point $P$; only odd-even pairs give distinct points.
questions.justification: Careful bookkeeping of which pairs meet and where; short once the idea is seen.

questions.key_step: All triples minus the collinear triples on each side.
questions.justification: One standard subtraction of collinear triples.

questions.key_step: Alphabetical order $B,B,H,J,O$; blocks $B\ldots,H\ldots,J\ldots$ use up $48$ words.
questions.justification: Block counting with a repeated letter, then reading the 2nd word of the last block.

questions.key_step: $S$ has $9$ elements; split into three labelled sets of $3$ each: $\frac{9!}{3!3!3!}$.
questions.justification: Count of ordered partitions; main risk is dividing by $3!$ when the sets are named.

questions.key_step: No two chosen vertices may be adjacent; the first-vertex count $8\times6=48$ counts each triangle three times.
questions.justification: A slip is easy (overcounting by $3$), the PDF itself ends on $48$; no direct formula familiar to most students.

questions.key_step: Alphabetical order $A,G,N,P,R,U$; subtract block sizes ($120,120,24,24,24$) then list the last three words.
questions.justification: Block subtraction then reading off three consecutive words; routine with distinct letters.

questions.key_step: Letters $M,A,T$ appear twice, the other five once; split by the repetition pattern (11111, 2111, 221).
questions.justification: Selection (not arrangement) from a multiset with three kinds of repetition pattern; easy to miss a pattern.

questions.key_step: Let group A give $a$ men (and $4-a$ women); then group B must give $4-a$ men and $a$ women.
questions.justification: Five cases with products of four binomials each; arithmetic precision.

questions.key_step: Count solutions of $x_1+..+x_4=16$ with $1\le x_i\le6$ by generating function / inclusion-exclusion.
questions.justification: Bounded stars and bars with two correction terms; numeric precision.

questions.key_step: Count all $3$-digit numbers ($60$) and subtract those whose digit sum is a multiple of $3$.
questions.justification: Complement with a small enumeration of triples; the triple list must be complete.

questions.key_step: Split by repetition pattern of the digits (all different, two alike) or use bounded stars and bars.
questions.justification: Precise casework with a zero-leading restriction; no options; a miscount is easy.
